entries.title: Hotel furniture and renovation projects
entries.summary: A hotel brings together different uses. Guestrooms need space for luggage, storage and circulation. Public spaces and dining areas need their own furniture choices. We review these requirements using your plans and room schedules.
sections: Define the scope by space
List room types and identify beds, headboards, desks and storage for each type. Schedule public spaces and restaurant furniture separately so proposals can be compared consistently.
Connect furniture with technical planning
Review dimensions, finishes, power points, lighting and assembly access together. Working drawings and samples should be confirmed before the order is approved.
Plan a phased renovation
Specify which areas are available, storage constraints and handover dates. Production, transport and on-site work are separate stages.

entries.title: Office furniture for your workplace project
entries.summary: Workplace projects begin with people and activities. Workstation counts, meeting spaces, circulation and storage needs provide a framework for selection. Hongye discusses configurations and finishes using your layout.
sections: Start with the layout
Specify team size, work patterns and spaces to furnish. Check access routes, door openings and the space around desks and tables.
Coordinate equipment
Define cable routes, displays, power points and conferencing equipment. Visually similar configurations can meet different technical requirements.
Compare specifications
Review dimensions, supports, finishes, adjustments and maintenance needs line by line. Required documents and tests should be identified for the selected models.

entries.title: Furniture for restaurants and social spaces
entries.summary: A restaurant combines guest comfort, staff movement and everyday use. Review seating capacity, table layouts and seat heights before choosing finishes. Lounges and bars need choices suited to their use.
sections: Plan the dining space
Separate two- and four-person tables, larger groups, bar areas and lounge seating. A zone-based schedule connects quantities to the plan.
Choose finishes for the use
Describe cleaning needs, stain exposure, frequency of use and colour references. Performance claims must be supported by documents for the product concerned.
Consider storage
For multifunctional spaces, specify stacking, movement and storage needs. Check access for replacing or maintaining items.

entries.title: Furniture for your villa project
entries.summary: A residential project benefits from an overall view. Room proportions, access, light and daily habits guide furniture choices. Fenmi Casa discusses selections using your plans, references and material palette.
sections: Build a shared direction
Gather style references and identify priority rooms. A palette of wood, fabrics and surfaces can connect living, dining and bedroom spaces without making every room identical.
Check dimensions
Compare furniture footprints with measured plans and access routes. Doors, stairs and lifts can affect handling and assembly.
Define what is included
Separate freestanding furniture, drawing-based items and accessories. Services, samples and delivery conditions are defined through the project brief.

entries.title: Furniture for apartments and private residences
entries.summary: Apartments require careful coordination between furniture and available space. Fenmi Casa discusses pieces, dimensions and finishes within a defined residential project.
sections: Respect the proportions
Review sofas, tables and beds on the plan. Circulation and openings must remain compatible with daily use.
Connect different spaces
Living and dining areas can share a palette while serving different functions. Tell us about existing finishes when discussing combinations.
Plan access
Provide lift dimensions, floor information and building access. On-site services are confirmed for the destination and agreed scope.

entries.title: A furniture contact for residential designers
entries.summary: Working with an interior designer depends on precise information. References, drawings, dimensions and samples provide the basis for coordination. Fenmi Casa helps organise furniture choices and the technical points to confirm.
sections: Structure the selection
Prepare a room-by-room list with references, desired sizes and inspiration images. Separate existing models from items needing further review.
Approve the finishes
Connect each finish with a reference and sample where needed. Decisions and document versions should remain traceable.
Review interfaces
Identify furniture adjoining walls, floors or equipment. Joinery work and local installation depend on the agreed scope, rather than a general promise.

entries.title: Hotel guestroom furniture set
entries.summary: Coordinate beds, headboards, desks and storage with the room type.

entries.title: Buffet and storage furniture
entries.summary: A storage selection for dining and service areas.

entries.title: Restaurant and dining table
entries.summary: Select table formats in relation to capacity and circulation.

entries.title: Bar and high seating
entries.summary: Review seat height against the actual counter and intended use.

entries.title: Workstation and modular layout
entries.summary: Review workstations against your workplace layout.

entries.title: Meeting-room table
entries.summary: Configure the table for room capacity, access and equipment.

entries.title: Reception desk
entries.summary: Review reception furniture around staff tasks and visitor movement.

entries.title: Residential living-room furniture
entries.summary: Coordinate seating and tables around your living-room plan.

entries.title: Bedroom and private-space furniture
entries.summary: Organise selections by room, dimensions and material palette.

entries.title: Furniture selection for private interiors
entries.summary: Coordinate residential furniture using a room-by-room brief.

entries.title: Furniture dimensions and customisation
entries.summary: Customisation connects your expectations with the constraints of the product. Plans, measurements, references and quantities help review options for your project.
sections: Review dimensions
Provide desired sizes, site measurements and wall or equipment interfaces. Feasibility is confirmed for the chosen model.
Record the decisions
Link every change to an item reference and document version. Changes after approval may affect production conditions.
Confirm the scope
Supply, additional studies and on-site work are defined in the proposal.

entries.title: Materials and finishes for your project
entries.summary: Materials are selected for appearance, use and maintenance. We review your references and the documentation needed for the products selected.
sections: Connect appearance with use
Describe frequency of use, cleaning needs and indoor or outdoor conditions. A visual finish alone does not demonstrate performance.
Compare references
Associate material names, colours, surfaces and sample references with the same item. Technical documents are reviewed for the relevant models.
Confirm with a sample
On-screen colour varies with lighting and displays. An approved sample provides a clearer reference for the order.

entries.title: Samples and project approval
entries.summary: Approval can concern a material, finish, drawing or model. Sample requirements are agreed according to the project and chosen products.
sections: Choose review points
Identify what needs review: appearance, dimensions, assembly, equipment or documents. Record the scope in the brief.
Record decisions
Use item references and version numbers for each decision. Avoid contradictory approvals between drawings, messages and samples.
Prepare the next stage
Quantities, finishes and schedule should be confirmed before ordering. Sample conditions and costs are discussed for your request.

entries.title: Preparing packing and delivery
entries.summary: Delivery planning starts with quantities, destination and site access. Transport, receiving and assembly conditions are confirmed within the agreed scope.
sections: Organise the batches
A room-, zone- or phase-based schedule can help identify packages. Specify storage needs and site readiness.
Clarify responsibilities
Transport, customs, taxes, unloading and assembly need separate discussion. A general price or delivery period cannot replace a destination-specific proposal.
Prepare receiving
Identify the receiving location, access and responsible people. Assembly documents and reporting conditions are defined for the order.

entries.title: Preparing a hotel furniture schedule
entries.summary: A useful schedule links each item to a space, quantity and reference. It helps teams review the scope and compare proposals.
sections: Start with the spaces
List room types, then reception, dining, meetings and other included areas. Keep typical-room quantities separate from total quantities.
Describe each item
Include function, desired dimensions, material, finish and quantity. Attach a plan or reference when an item depends on a layout.
Separate the services
Samples, transport, receiving and installation should be identified with their responsibilities. Furniture quotations can cover different scopes.

entries.title: Preparing your residential furniture brief
entries.summary: An initial brief does not need to be complete. It should explain the rooms, preferences and decisions already made.
sections: Describe the rooms
List rooms to furnish and furniture to retain. Measured plans and access dimensions help frame the selection.
Share references
A few style images and a material palette are more useful than many unexplained pictures. Say what you like about each reference.
Identify priorities
Destination, target date and room priorities help discuss the schedule. Delivery and services are defined for your brief.

entries.title: Organising sample approval
entries.summary: Clear approval connects a decision with an item, version and responsible person. This reduces uncertainty across documents.
sections: Identify the reference
Describe the item, material and finish. Record the date and reference of the reviewed sample.
Describe the decision
State whether the sample is approved, requires changes or needs another review. Record specific reservations in the brief.
Keep versions consistent
After a change, verify that drawings and furniture schedules use the same version. Photographs do not replace every physical check.

entries.title: Comparing furniture quotations on a common basis
entries.summary: Quotations are comparable only when their scopes are comparable. A lower total may reflect different materials, quantities or services.
sections: Compare the items
Check dimensions, finishes, quantities and composition. A product name alone does not establish equivalence.
Identify services
Samples, packing, transport, importation and assembly may be included, excluded or priced separately. Check each proposal.
Document open questions
Review substitutions, documents, stage-by-stage timing, payment terms and responsibilities before approval. Estimates must remain distinct from contractual conditions.

entries.title: Information for an office furniture project
entries.summary: The brief should explain who uses the spaces, what equipment is needed and how furniture fits the plan.
sections: Describe activities
Specify headcount, fixed or shared desks, meeting capacity and reception needs.
Define interfaces
Identify cable routes, screens and equipment. Check access and storage.
Prepare specifications
Define desired dimensions, finishes and documentation. Performance is confirmed for selected models.

entries.title: Phasing a hotel renovation: guestrooms, reception and dining
entries.summary: Hotel renovations are rarely delivered in one phase. Splitting the work by space — guestrooms, reception, dining — keeps the property trading and lets you compare proposals on the same scope.
sections: Why split the renovation by space

The split follows how the property operates, not how a catalogue is arranged. A guestroom wing can close while reception stays in service; the reverse is rarely possible. For each space, record downtime windows, on-site storage constraints and assembly access before you compare proposals.
Start with the guestrooms

Guestrooms carry the largest and most repetitive volume. Group them by room type and list beds, headboards, desks and storage for each type. One approved type becomes the reference for the rest; surface differences are handled afterwards, not at the point of order.
Plan the reception and public areas

Reception brings together a welcome zone, a working position and a circulation route. Counter dimensions, cable routes and accessibility requirements are reviewed against the plan, because a visually similar layout can serve a different use.
Set the restaurant and dining areas

Covers, service style and storage drive the selection. Tables, seating and buffet units are reviewed together: a table selected for the dining room will not necessarily suit the terrace or breakfast service.
Allocate responsibilities and stages

Production, transport, receiving, installation and packing removal are separate stages. Each appears in the brief with its own responsibility. That level of detail prevents two quotations from being read as the same scope.

entries.title: Hotel guestroom furniture: what actually changes across service tiers
entries.summary: Three-star, four-star, boutique or five-star: the gap is not mainly a matter of style, but of what survives use. Two units that look alike may carry 0.4 mm or 2 mm edging, a roller runner or a full-extension runner with soft close. The markers below describe ranges seen in hotel work and are to be confirmed against supplier documentation. Here are the points that genuinely change, and how to turn them into parameters you can inspect before comparing proposals. These markers are there to frame the right questions, not to rank a supplier.
sections: Tier shows first in the carcass

An entry-level unit often uses 16 mm particleboard with 0.4 to 0.8 mm applied edging. A higher tier moves to 18 or 19 mm board with 1.5 to 2 mm ABS edging, laid flat or flush. Band thickness matters as much as the adhesive: thin edging lifts at the first suitcase knock, and the repair shows. Behind the front, the runner decides the feel — roller, ball-bearing, then full extension with soft close. Ask for the rated load per pair, the travel and the cycle count tested. The back panel, often a thin stapled sheet, deserves the same scrutiny as the face, particularly when it carries drawers. Adjustable shelves on pins, rather than fixed battens, let a cabinet be reconfigured without tools, and that flexibility belongs in the brief. Fixings count too: wood screws in a soft board, cam fittings or inserts in a dense one. Specifying by brand name alone leaves the tier open to interpretation, so describe the assembly instead.
Fabrics, foam and removability

Abrasion resistance is read in Martindale rubs. A lightly used guestroom often holds between 20,000 and 25,000 rubs; a standard hotel room sits nearer 30,000 to 40,000; heavily used seating goes beyond 50,000. These figures are checked on the supplier's report, not on the label. Fire treatment and its classification are confirmed against the regulations of the destination country. A removable cover changes maintenance: closure type, fabric direction, washing behaviour and dimensional stability. For foam, 30 to 40 kg/m³ suits a back panel; a seat calls for a firmer density and a worked thickness, and the two should be specified separately. One spare cover per room type avoids taking a room out of service for a single stain, so state the washing regime you expect. Pile direction and shade are checked on a fitted cover, not on a sample lying flat. State whether covers are washed in-house or contracted out, because that changes the closure and the seam allowance.
The bed: frame, headboard and support

The bed concentrates the most expensive things to correct. A basic frame butts panels together; a higher tier uses solid wood or plywood legs, corner brackets, a central rail and adjustable feet. Beech or birch slats sit in holders that limit squeaking: their number and section matter more than their finish. Headboards fix in three ways — wall rail, integrated into the frame, or suspended — and a wall rail, which limits vibration, depends on the wall build-up. The mattress support, whether slats, a base or a platform, has to be described: it drives comfort and the replacement route later on. Headboard height follows the mattress top rather than the mood board: give it as a dimension from finished floor and check it against the bedside table. A close-slatted base and a sprung base are replaced differently once the floor is trading. Ask how the headboard is accessed for reupholstery without removing the bed.
Hardware, lighting and power points

Hardware decides how the room feels in use. A damped hinge with three-axis adjustment can be reset after settlement; a plain hinge only opens. Handles hold through bolted fixings or inserts: adhesive alone gives way. Mirrors integrate side or perimeter lighting, with colour temperature and colour rendering stated, and the ingress protection rating matters in the bathroom. On the electrical side, a guestroom needs sockets at the bedside, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a free point for a charger. These details weigh little at design stage and a great deal to add later, once the walls are closed. A cable route cut at machining stage avoids drilling on site and the making good that follows, so show it on the furniture drawing. Door buffers and drawer bumpers cut noise, which matters along a corridor at night. Bedside controls should be reachable from the pillow without stretching.
Storage, maintenance and the specification

Storage is drawn from use: rail height, number of adjustable shelves, internal drawers, wardrobe lighting, space for a suitcase and for a safe. A luggage rack is chosen for its height and load, not its look. A minibar needs a ventilated niche and a dedicated socket. Maintenance is prepared at order stage: removable fronts, replaceable panels, interchangeable headboard covers, identified spare parts. Five-year serviceability is judged on those possibilities, not on a promise. Finally, the specification translates tier into parameters: board and edging thickness, runner load and travel, rub count, foam density, fixing method. Those are the values that get inspected on delivery. A spares schedule with references and quantities is handed over with the room file, and that document is what keeps a floor running in year four. Safe niche dimensions and usable wardrobe depth are measured on site, not taken from the architect’s plan. Photograph the inside of a finished wardrobe; it is the part guests judge daily.
checklist: Board and edging thickness in millimetres
Runner load rating, travel and cycle count
Martindale rub count and fire treatment class
Foam density and removable cover specification
Headboard fixing method and wall build-up
Wardrobe, safe, minibar and power point positions

entries.title: How many covers to plan for before ordering restaurant furniture
entries.summary: The cover count is settled before the tables are chosen, not after. A room sized by eye and then furnished often ends up with aisles that are too tight or rows that cannot be sold, and a layout is hard to correct once the furniture is ordered. Area, deductions, table formats and circulation turn into a simple schedule that every proposal can follow and challenge. The aim is not to fill the room, but to reach a cover count that holds up in service. Here is how to move from floor area to a number of covers, and which margins to check on site before the order is fixed.
sections: Start from usable seating area, not total floor area

A 180 m² dining room does not offer 180 m² of seats. Deduct the bar, the buffet, service stations, exits and circulation first, then apply 1.2 to 1.8 m² per cover for table service, or 0.9 to 1.2 m² for quick service and cafés. These figures are planning references, not a delivery commitment: room shape, columns, banquettes and the chosen furniture all change the result. For example, 180 m² less 25 m² of bar, 18 m² of buffet and 20 per cent circulation leaves about 110 m² of seating, or 60 to 90 covers depending on the comfort level sought. Keep the density consistent with the service you advertise, and calculate a terrace separately.
Choose table formats that can be combined

A 700 to 800 mm square table seats two; two of them pushed together make a four, provided the bases do not clash and the tops line up. A 1200 to 1400 mm by 800 mm rectangular table does the same job without handling. A round table of 1200 to 1400 mm in diameter seats four to six and softens the corners of a room. A long table suits groups and narrow rooms. Check the height under the top, usually 720 to 750 mm, and the footprint of the bases, which decides real legroom. Mixing formats only helps if heights, edges and finishes stay compatible, and if a split pair does not block an aisle.
Set the aisles and the clearances

Three widths structure the room: 1200 mm for the main aisle, 900 mm for the service aisle, and 900 mm between the table edge and the wall so a chair can be pulled out. Between two occupied tables, allow 900 to 1000 mm from chair back to chair back; below that, guests rise sideways and service slows down. These are working minimums: check them on a scaled plan with the actual furniture, and against the accessibility and fire safety rules that apply to the premises. Add fixed obstacles — columns, radiators, doors — before counting. A 1200 mm aisle on paper can become 600 mm once chairs are pulled out.
Service style changes the arithmetic

Plated service holds a table for longer than a buffet or a counter does. The cover count therefore cannot be read from floor area alone: it depends on how long guests stay and how many services you run. Estimate turnover per service, then check that the kitchen and bar can keep up; adding covers without extra kitchen throughput simply moves the wait into the dining room. Bar seating counts differently: a stool takes less floor than a table but stays occupied for longer. An all-day lobby bar is not sized like a dinner room. Count standing places and stools as separate categories, not as tables, and note that a counter turns faster at lunch than at dinner.
Terrace, breakfast and the seating table

On a terrace and at breakfast, furniture has to move, stack and withstand exposure. Allow a store or a corner for tables that are not in use, and check the weight of each piece if staff handle it alone. Anticipate wind, sun and rain, which drive the choice of materials and the storage arrangement. At breakfast, density can be higher and occupancy shorter. Then set out a table by zone: gross area, deductions, table formats, resulting covers. That table becomes the reference document for comparing proposals; the five points in the checklist still need confirming on site. Loose furniture also makes cleaning and evening re-sets easier.
checklist: Zone table: gross area, deductions, formats, covers obtained
Target covers per service and expected turnover, bar and terrace included
Aisle widths measured on site, not only on the plan
Bar, buffet and service stations positioned before counting
Terrace: storage, stacking, exposure, weight of pieces

entries.title: Hotel Lobby Furniture: Zones, Circulation and Selection
entries.summary: A lobby is not a room furnished in one gesture. It is a sequence of moments a guest crosses in seconds, suitcase in hand. Reception, waiting, work, bar and the circulation spine share neither the same clear widths, nor the same fabrics, nor the same service life. The markers below are ranges seen in hotel work and are to be confirmed on plan and against supplier documentation. They are there to frame the right questions before comparing proposals, not to rank a supplier.
sections: Read the lobby as five zones, not one room

A lobby is read on foot, not from a plan. From the entrance to the desk, then from the desk to the lifts, a guest passes through at least four atmospheres in a few seconds: he puts down a case, looks for a reference point, waits, sometimes sits, orders a coffee, leaves. Each moment calls for different furniture and, above all, a different clear width. Splitting the lobby into five zones — arrival, waiting, work and social, bar, circulation spine — stops the room being treated as one batch of seating.

The method needs three surveys. First the spine: the most direct line between entrance, reception and lifts, kept at 1.20 m clear minimum, widening to 1.50 m at crossings and in front of the queue. Then the contact points: hands on armrests, cases against benches, trays set on low tables. Finally the dimensions of each group, taken between furniture rather than between walls, because a chair pushed back 20 cm eats a passage.

That split has a direct consequence for the tender pack. A lobby specified with one fabric and one foam density will be over-specified in the quiet corners and under-specified around the bar. Separating the zones lets each carry its own rub count, its own cover type and its own replacement logic, without paying twice for the same performance.
Arrival and reception: the first three metres

The arrival zone carries the hardest-working furniture in the lobby: reception desk, counter return, low console, luggage bench, high stools for standing waits, umbrella stand. The worktop usually sits between 1,050 and 1,150 mm, with an accessible position at 750–800 mm, 700 mm clear knee width and 450 mm knee depth. In front of the desk, allow 1,200 mm clear for a guest with a case and a companion; behind it, 900 mm for the chair and staff movement. A luggage bench sits at 450–500 mm seat height, 400–450 mm deep, with a top protected by an applied edge.

The desk front takes trolleys, cases and belt buckles. A high-pressure laminate face or a veneer with 2 mm ABS edging can be repaired locally; a lacquer far less so. Treat the plinth as a wear part: removable kick plate, through-bolted fixings, a colour close to the floor to hide scuffs. High stools in the waiting position need vinyl at 50,000 Martindale minimum, a seat with no seam across the front, and replaceable glides.

One detail is often missed: the queue. Without a floor line or a drop-off bench, guests stop at the desk and block the spine. A waiting seat 1,500 mm from the desk, or a 400 mm deep console for bags, often clears it. Add a socket near the bench and lighting that makes the desk readable without glare in the eyes of someone seated.
Waiting: set the spacing before choosing the chair

In the waiting zone, comfort comes down to simple dimensions. A lobby armchair sits at 420–450 mm, is 480–520 mm deep and allows 600–700 mm width per place. Between two chairs, a 400–450 mm diameter side table needs 400–450 mm clear on each side. Two chairs facing each other sit 800–900 mm apart so knees do not touch; behind the backs, allow 1,200 mm where the circulation spine runs. Check these on a 1:20 plan, not on a mood image.

Waiting upholstery works through prolonged contact rather than hard abrasion: 40,000 to 50,000 Martindale for a lobby seat, 25,000 to 30,000 for a back. Seat foam at 35–40 kg/m³ holds its shape; below that the seat compacts and the front edge collapses. A removable cover with a concealed closure and the pile running the right way lets a cushion be turned or replaced without taking the group out of service. A pale velvet soils at the back and armrests: choose a mid-tone or a tight weave.

The real cost of lobby seating is not read at order stage but at the first replacement. Three decisions reduce it: cushions independent of the back, covers available separately, a demountable frame. In use, cushions turn, covers wash, a frame is repaired without scrapping the seat. A fully upholstered and glued seat, by contrast, forces the whole chair out for one stain or one local collapse.
Work and social: a table that takes a laptop

The work-and-social zone now hosts mixed uses: a guest answering messages, two colleagues preparing a meeting, a traveller waiting for a taxi. A bar-height table does not work for seated laptop use; 740–750 mm height, 600 mm usable depth per person and 700 mm seat width remain the baseline. For a shared table, allow 600 mm width per place and 1,200 mm between back-to-back rows once chairs are pushed back. A fixed banquette saves space but requires the seat depth (450–480 mm) and the table clearance (250–300 mm) to be calculated.

Power points decide the real use. Two sockets per table, one of them USB-C, with a cable route cut at machining stage rather than drilled on site, remove visible extension leads. The top should stay matt under lighting: a glossy laminate throws the screen back. On acoustics, a stone-and-glass lobby sends conversation towards reception; absorbent panels under table tops or inside seats, plus heavy textiles, lower the level without dividing the room.

In the social zone, table edges, armrests and backs wear first. A 2 mm edge, a top replaceable independently of the base and armrests supplied as separate parts change the maintenance bill over time. Avoid tops bonded permanently to the base: one deep scratch then means removing the whole table.
Bar and circulation spine: what fails first

Around the bar, dimensions start from the counter. For a counter at 1,050–1,100 mm, a stool sets at 750–780 mm seat height, with a footrest around 450 mm. Allow 250–300 mm between stools, a 300–350 mm counter overhang for the knees, and 1,200 mm clear behind occupied stools — more where a stool pulls back. Without that overhang, knees meet the face of the counter, the guest sits at an angle and the seat edge wears.

The main spine stays at 1,200 mm, widening to 1,500 mm at crossings, in front of the lifts and at the restaurant entrance. Low furniture — consoles, planters, display stands — belongs outside that spine, at least 300 mm from door leaves. Floor changes need a flat profile: a poorly set threshold bar trips guests and tears the glides off stools.

The bar stool is the most-replaced item in a lobby: seat edge, seams, glides, footrest. Technical vinyl at 100,000 Martindale, a moulded seat with no seam across the front and a metal frame with screwed glides last better than furnishing fabric. Finally, separate quantities by zone and wear parts in the tender pack: seats, covers, tops, glides. That separation is what allows one batch of stools to be replaced without touching the waiting chairs, and keeps a lobby coherent after several years of trading.
checklist: Clear width of the main spine and crossings
Reception worktop and accessible counter heights
Seat spacing and clearance behind armchairs
Martindale rub count by zone and removable covers
Sockets, cable routes and foot protection

entries.title: Hotel lobby furniture: what moves the quote
entries.summary: Two quotes prepared for lobbies of comparable size can diverge widely, and the gap is almost never explained by the manufacturer’s margin alone. It comes from what each quote understands by “lobby furniture”: which families are included, at what customization level, with which internal specifications and which services. This guide breaks those factors down so the proposals can be brought back to a comparable basis.
sections: Why do two quotes for the same lobby diverge?

The first cause is scope. A quote covering seating, tables, the reception desk and accessories is not comparable to one limited to seating: the rest reappears later as add-on costs. The second cause is the customization level; an adjusted catalogue piece is not priced like an original drawing with a dedicated prototype and sample. The third gathers the invisible specifications — frame, cushioning, testing — that the mood image never shows. The fourth is logistics: packaging, transport and site reception can stay outside the displayed amount.
Which furniture families should the quote include?

A complete quote names each family on its own line: waiting and lounge seating, coffee and side tables, the reception desk, and accessories such as a luggage bench, space divider, planters or a coat stand. Each family carries its quantity and its control document: a workshop drawing for the reception desk, a material sheet for the seating, a packing scheme for the whole set. A quote that does not cite the document usually has not budgeted what it covers. Preparing the lobby with the same method as the hotel furniture schedule prevents omissions that turn into supplements.
Customization: catalogue, adapted or bespoke?

Three levels coexist. Catalogue adjustment keeps the existing design and changes only the fabric, lacquer or wood tone; tooling is shared across projects. Adaptation changes dimensions, adds a socket or reinforces a structure; extra preparation is added. Bespoke starts from your drawings: a prototype, a dedicated sample and committee validation before the series. The common mistake is to ask for a “distinctive style” with a catalogue budget; when the committee validates an original drawing at the third round, the prototype rework returns as a separate line if the quote excluded it.
Which invisible specifications weigh on the price?

Three layers escape the presentation image. Structure first: frame sections, material and reinforcements at the support points; intensive-use seating is designed for non-domestic usage tests. Comfort next: foam density and height, the suspension system and the resilience of the filling; high-resilience foam keeps its shape after thousands of cycles and its raw material shows in the quote. Compliance finally: the fire behaviour of the fabrics and the lot documents that allow each batch to be traced. To check this layer, require a technical sheet that cites the test, a physical sample approved against that document, and the right to inspect during production.
How to bring two quotes to a common basis?

Before placing two amounts side by side, align five points: family scope, customization level, seating specification, packing standard and delivery term. Each gap becomes a precise question: are the prototype and the sample included or billed separately, is export packing inside the price, which on-site works stay separate. The detailed method for comparing quotations on a common basis provides the framework; applied to the lobby, it turns a price gap into a list of different scopes.
Which costs appear after the signature?

Three sources recur. Packaging and transport: a figure on FOB terms covers neither the container, nor the insurance, nor the delivery to site. Installation: a lobby is fitted in a hotel in operation or in an opening on a tight schedule, with service-lift and night-work constraints. Revision rounds: every change after the approved sample reopens production, and quotes limit the number of free rounds. Ask for that number to be written in the quote, not in a later email.
checklist: Technical sheet with cited test for seating

entries.title: Hotel headboard wall: power outlets, reading lights and wall protection
entries.summary: The headboard wall concentrates, on a few square metres, most of the rework reported after a guest room opens: an outlet nobody can reach, a reading lamp aimed at the reader's face, a finish marked by rolled headboards. The cause is almost never the furniture itself; it is late coordination between the electrical plan, the furniture shop drawings and the choice of finishes. This article sets out the decisions to settle on plan, in which order, and which documents to freeze before ordering.
sections: Why is the headboard wall decided before the bed is chosen?

In a hotel guest room the headboard wall is not decoration; it is an interface. On one side sit joinery and upholstery, on the other electrical points, lighting control and finishes that must survive daily use. Until the bed width, the nightstand positions and the headboard overhang are fixed, outlet and lamp positions remain hanging. If the electrician works ahead of the shop drawings, points end up behind solid panels or, worse, inside the volume a nightstand hides. The correct order is therefore: room layout frozen, wall shop drawings approved, then electrical points transferred onto the wall elevation. That sequence removes most rework and applies to renovation as much as to new build.
At what height should outlets and reading lights be mounted?

Usual heights are settled on plan, together with the electrician and the architect, from three references: finished floor level, the top of the mattress or made-up bed, and the top of the nightstand. An outlet set too low becomes unreachable once the headboard is installed; a lamp set too high lights the reader's face instead of the page. The reliable method is to draw the wall at true scale, trace a seated reader on it, and place every point relative to that silhouette rather than to the bare wall. Each project then fixes its own dimensions; they are frozen on the execution drawing and checked on the mock-up before series production.
Reading lights: what aiming and what control?

A hotel reading lamp is judged on three things: beam aim, control, and independence of each side. The beam must light the page without crossing the bed axis; it is the lamp body orientation, more than its output, that decides comfort. Control must be reachable without sitting up, from the seated position, and independent of the room's master switch. Finally, each side of the bed is switched separately: two guests do not read at the same time. On plan these requirements translate into one technical sheet per luminaire and one control point per side, transferred onto the wall elevation together with the furniture shop drawings.
Wall protection: what should be specified above and around the bed?

The most stressed band of the wall is the one no render shows: the strip where heads rest, where luggage leans during housekeeping, where the bed runner rubs at every turn-down. Finishes there are chosen to be washable and repairable: lacquered timber panels or laminates for the frame, coated technical fabrics for soft surfaces, fold-down protection behind the headboard where connecting rooms are planned. The specification separates the contact zone, which receives the toughest finish, from the upper bands, which can be more decorative. These zones are defined line by line on the elevation, and every finish is validated by an approved sample against a document.
How is the wall coordinated with the furniture on plan?

Coordination happens on a single view: the headboard wall elevation, on which the headboard, nightstands, electrical points and lamps are overlaid. Three checks are systematic. First, does each outlet axis fall outside the volume hidden by the headboard and outside the volume occupied by the nightstand? Second, does the nightstand top edge leave the outlet reachable without moving furniture? Third, have the joinery installation tolerances (a few millimetres per panel) absorbed the allowance needed for cable routes? This one view, signed by both the furniture and electrical packages before ordering, replaces weeks of email loops during installation.
Which documents should be frozen before ordering?

Four documents are enough to secure a headboard wall. The dimensioned architectural plan of the room, which provides the height references. The coordinated electrical plan, where every point is numbered and transferred onto the wall elevation. The furniture shop drawings with dimensioned sections, which show what the joinery hides and what it leaves accessible. And the sign-off report of the mock-up, which validates a sample room in the workshop or on site before series production. As a space reference, a hotel project in Zanzibar (Tanzania) documents guest rooms whose headboard walls combine timber panels, wall lamps and floating nightstands; those images serve to discuss compositions, they do not describe a delivery in any specific country and involve no brand.
checklist: Wall layout dimensioned on the architectural plan
Electrical points: outlets, USB, switches coordinated
Reading lights: model, aiming, control per side
Protection finishes by contact zone and upper band
Furniture alignment: headboard and nightstands on one elevation
Mock-up and signed validation report before series

entries.title: FF&E specifications: structuring a hotel tender
entries.summary: An FF&E tender is decided before it is sent: in how the brief splits packages, sets quantities by room type and describes finishes. When those three points stay vague, replies arrive on different scopes and comparing prices stops meaning anything. This article sets out a brief structure that lets you compare, negotiate and receive without starting the analysis again.
sections: Why does the package split decide how offers can be compared?

A hotel project mixes furniture families with different tolerances, lead times and installation constraints: guestrooms, bathrooms, reception, restaurant, meeting rooms and corridors. Sent as one package, the tender forces every manufacturer to price items it does not produce, so the returned figure becomes an assembly price that is hard to audit. Split into packages, it can be compared line by line and the gap becomes visible immediately.

A workable split follows three rules: one package per technical family (guestroom furniture, upholstered seating, restaurant furniture, joinery), one package per zone where finishes differ strongly, and a separate package for installation and logistics. Each package carries its own schedule, finishes and exclusions, so a reply cannot hide behind a neighbouring item. The split also makes the mock-up clause negotiable, because a sample room can be signed off package by package on different dates.
How do you set quantities by room type without getting it wrong?

Quantities are read by room type, never as one global total. A 120-key hotel can hold four or five types with different layouts: standard, accessible, superior and suite. The schedule must list, for each type, the composition item by item, then multiply by the number of keys. That matrix, not a total, is what later drives the delivery check.

Two columns prevent most disputes: contracted quantity and reserve quantity. The reserve covers site breakage, sample rooms and replacement during the first months of operation. It must be stated in the brief, otherwise each manufacturer interprets it differently and may or may not include it in the price. Quantities must also be tied to a dated drawing revision; a schedule without a drawing reference becomes unusable at the first architect revision.
What belongs in the finishes schedule?

The finishes schedule is the document that links the drawing to the price. For each element it lists the surface reference, colour, grain direction, edge type, hardware and expected resistance level. Without it, two manufacturers price two different qualities under the same label of pale oak, and the price gap measures only the material gap.

Best practice is one visual reference per finish, with a version number and a date, and variants priced separately as options so they can be arbitrated at the end of negotiation without reopening the whole schedule. Technical finishes such as fire performance of upholstery, cleanability of surfaces and edge protection need their own section: they are compliance requirements, not colours, and should be presented as such.
How should the mock-up room clause be written?

The mock-up room turns a brief into an enforceable reference. The clause must state the exact content, item by item, with the selected finishes; the lead time after shop drawings are approved; and the validation process, meaning who inspects, who signs, within what period, and what happens if a reservation is raised.

One point is often missed: a mock-up room is only a reference if it is photographed and documented at signature. The minutes should include photographs, finish references and any tolerances accepted. That document, not the memory of the participants, serves for checking the following rooms. The clause should also cover reversibility: whether the room returns to operation, is dismantled, or its items are reused, since each option has a cost that belongs in the offer.
On what criteria should replies be evaluated?

An evaluation grid written before offers are opened keeps the decision from resting on price alone. The useful criteria are few but must be weighted: compliance with the schedule, quality and consistency of proposed finishes, ability to hold the programme, comparable project references, warranty and after-sales terms, and then price.

Two criteria decide hotel projects. The first is clarity of exclusions: an offer that does not state what it leaves out will be completed by variations. The second is the quality control method announced: inspection plan, acceptance criteria and how non-conformities are handled. A manufacturer who describes the method is easier to manage than one who promises an outcome. The grid should also provide a provisional ranking and a question phase, because a poorly written reply can hide a solid offer.
Which exclusions must be stated in writing?

The exclusion list protects both sides. It must state what is not included: unloading and handling on site, storage, assembly, electrical connections, floor and paint repairs after installation, removal of packaging, and training of floor staff. Each of these has a real cost and will eventually be claimed by someone.

The brief must also list interfaces: who supplies the lighting, who drills walls for sockets, who adjusts cabinet doors after the finished floor is laid. Unassigned interfaces are the first cause of delay on hotel sites, well ahead of manufacturing lead times. An interface table with an owner column and a reference document column is usually enough: it is short, it reads in five minutes, and it removes entire site meetings.
checklist: One package per technical family and finish zone, each with its own schedule
Quantities by room type, with contracted and reserve quantities
A dated drawing reference for every schedule
A versioned finishes schedule with one visual reference per finish
Mock-up clause: content, lead time, validation, reservations, reversibility
A weighted evaluation grid written before offers are opened
An exclusions and interfaces table with owner and reference document

entries.title: Mobilier de terrasse et de piscine pour hôtels : matériaux et fixations
entries.summary: A lounger that creaks in its third season, a table rusting at the base, a parasol tipping over at the first gust: on a pool deck these incidents are not settled by a claim, they are settled by early replacement. Hotel terrace furniture is therefore handled as a technical package, with four decisions locked before the tender: the material family, the fixing type, the connection to the ground and the coherence across terrace, pool deck and garden. What follows does not rank materials by prestige: it ranks them by what they actually withstand over some ten years of operation, salt, chlorine, UV and daily handling included.
sections: Which materials best resist salt, chlorine and UV on a hotel terrace?

No material resists everything: teak and black locust hold up to salt water but suffer from neglected maintenance, aluminium tolerates chlorine and washing but concentrates the risk in its fixings, and woven resin resists UV only if its HDPE is stabilised and its frame remains aluminium. The choice between these four material families is therefore made by elimination according to real exposure, not by a hierarchy of prestige. Teak (Tectona grandis) owes its reputation to two wood compounds: tectoquinone, which limits insect attack, and a silica content that seals the surface against water while wearing out tools. On a hotel terrace this translates into a service life generally between ten and fifteen years without fungicide, provided the timber comes from a managed plantation and is properly dried before machining. Teak dried too fast moves, opens its joints and turns white in patches from the first season. The moisture content of the batch is checked before machining, generally 8 to 12% depending on origin, and batches above the upper limit are refused, even when the price per cubic metre is attractive. A chain-of-custody certification such as FSC does not cover this point: it documents origin, not drying. Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia), sold as false acacia, grows in Central Europe. Its hardness exceeds teak and its natural durability places it in use class 4 without treatment, allowing direct ground contact. It greys faster and takes on a silvery tone close to aged teak, with no oiling. Two operating reservations matter: weight, which complicates end-of-season handling, and checking, frequent on insufficiently stabilised solid sections. Aluminium 6060 or 6063, T6 treated then powder-coated, is the easiest material to operate on a pool deck: it does not rust, does not swell, accepts hosing and diluted chlorine, and stacks without splitting. Two points are checked at order: coating thickness, generally 60 to 80 µm for class 2, and the treatment of cut edges, because a bare cut becomes the entry point for filiform corrosion, especially in the coastal band. Surface temperature rises fast in the sun; on seating, weaving or textile remains necessary. Woven resin means HDPE yarns woven around a core, and quality depends not on the pattern but on three parameters: UV stabilisation of the HDPE, an aluminium core, and solution-dyed yarn. In a tender, the only useful question remains: can the supplier produce the test report of the delivered batch, not the one from the trade-show collection? In summary: teak — very good by the sea if drying is controlled, optional oiling and gentle cleaning, 10 to 15 years depending on exposure, main limitation price and batch variability; black locust — very good, use class 4, no oiling, 12 to 18 years observed, main limitations weight and checking; powder-coated aluminium — good, cut edges to protect, washing with water and neutral soap, 10 to 15 years depending on the finish, main limitation corrosion at the fixings; woven resin — good if HDPE is stabilised, hose cleaning without solvent, 5 to 9 years on the most exposed pieces, main limitation weaving replacement.
Teak, black locust, aluminium or woven resin: what is the ten-year operating cost?

Over ten years, the purchase price is only part of the spend: teak costs more upfront and little to maintain if the silvered look is accepted, aluminium costs less and needs almost nothing, woven resin costs the least but is replaced earlier on the most exposed pieces. The right indicator is therefore not the unit price but the full operating cost over the seasons actually served. Three cost items weigh heavily and disappear from price comparisons. The first is storage labour: a 12–18 kg solid-wood lounger takes two people, a 6–9 kg aluminium lounger takes one, and this difference becomes staff hours every evening of high season. The second is parasol mast breakage, often costlier than seating breakage, because a fallen parasol takes the neighbouring table with it. The third is replacement logistics: a part available in 45 to 60 days gets replaced, a part available in six months condemns the area. On a project in Doha (Qatar), a batch of woven-resin tables bought for their price lasted three seasons on the pool deck, then were replaced by aluminium tops and better-quality woven seating: the initial saving had been absorbed by two replacement campaigns and the time spent handling complaints. The same pattern returns in Muscat (Oman) on pieces left outside all year without shade. There is nonetheless a cost argument that holds: at equal specification, direct factory supply often sits 30 to 50% below a European brand quotation, provided documented quality control and a 45 to 60 day production lead time are accepted. The comparison only makes sense if the specification is identical on both sides: same profile thickness, same coating class, same assembly quality and same timber moisture control. On an indicative ten-year model, acquisition accounts for roughly 55–65% of total cost in teak, 50–60% in black locust, 60–70% in aluminium and 45–55% in woven resin; maintenance and cleaning 15–20% in teak and resin, 10–15% in black locust and aluminium; part replacement 10–15% for the first three families and 20–30% for resin; storage labour 5–10% in teak and aluminium, 10–15% in black locust and resin. This model is recalculated with the project's volumes and hourly rates, since the ranges vary with exposure and season length. The tiering logic described for hotel guestroom furniture applies outdoors too, with one extra criterion: the most exposed piece is not the one receiving the most guests, it is the one that stays in sun and spray all year.
Which fixings to choose per substrate: concrete slab, joist, gravel or lawn?

Fixings are chosen per substrate, not per habit: a concrete slab accepts a mechanical or chemical anchor in A4 stainless steel, a composite joist requires a countersunk A4 stainless screw with pre-drilling, gravel calls for a ballasted base without anchoring, and lawn a stake or a load-spreading plate. Each substrate has its own load-path logic, and these fixings rarely transfer from one substrate to another. On concrete, the critical point is not the anchor but the edge distance: an anchor set too close to a slab edge cracks the concrete before it holds, and the crack becomes a water path. A dimensioned anchoring plan is requested, with rebar positions where drawings exist, and a four-point base plate is preferred over a central foot on wind-exposed terrace tables. Right next to the pool, chemical anchoring remains possible but becomes delicate: resin dislikes a damp substrate and chlorine attacks some formulations; a ballasted, removable base plate avoids the problem. On composite or timber joists, countersunk A4 stainless screws with pre-drilling are the baseline; composite moves with temperature and a screw set without pre-drilling opens a crack that lengthens over one summer. Hidden clip fixings work on decking boards, not on load-bearing structures. On a timber deck, the washer matters as much as the screw: a washer too small marks the wood, a non-isolated stainless washer creates a galvanic couple with the aluminium of the base. On gravel and sand, no point anchoring is reliable: the solution is a heavy base, precast concrete or a fillable tray, whose mass is calculated from the wind load of the piece. On lawn, aim for a through stake or a buried spreading plate; with automatic irrigation the stake rises and the piece tips. Finally, on pool coping, drilling is almost always a bad idea: coping is often glued and drilling opens a water path under the tiling. A ballasted base set on the coping, with a soft glide, solves the need without touching the waterproofing. Summarised per substrate: concrete slab — 4-point base plate and A4 stainless anchor, avoid an anchor near the edge, check edge distance with a dimensioned plan; composite joist — A4 stainless screw with pre-drilling, avoid zinc-plated wood screws, check for crack initiation; gravel and sand — ballasted base or fillable tray, avoid a stake without a mass, check mass and wind load; lawn — through stake or spreading plate, avoid a simply set foot, check hold after watering; pool coping — ballasted base and soft glide, avoid drilling the coping, check waterproofing and level.
How to choose feet and glides for wind, standing water and cleaning?

Feet transfer three things to the ground: weight, lateral wind load, and the water running down the leg; choosing glides therefore means trading off slip, grip and drainage, with levelling adjusters compensating the slopes of a pool deck. A glide chosen to protect tiling can, at the same time, make the furniture unstable on a wet deck. The first trap is the felt glide, common on indoor pieces and disastrous outside: it absorbs water, swells, detaches and leaves a ring on stone. The second is the black filled-rubber glide, which migrates on light decks and leaves marks that are hard to remove. Drainage matters as much as material: an open-bottom tubular leg draws in water by capillarity, keeps it in the profile and releases it as a rust stain at the weld. Legs are delivered with closed end caps and drainage holes drilled at the lowest point, and this detail is verified on the assembly sheet rather than on the photo. On a project in Nice (France), a batch of tables delivered with simply pushed-in end caps saw, after one winter, trapped water burst the powder coating at the base; replacing the end caps cost less than reworking the frames. Wind is handled at the base, not the canopy: a 3 m parasol on a base of about twenty kilos lies down at the first storm, whatever the fabric quality. Water-fillable bases are practical in summer and awkward in winter, when freezing water splits the tray; sand weighs more per volume but travels badly. For stackable seating, a strap or shrink film over the stack prevents the sail effect. Finally, removable covers with quick-drain foam dry in about an hour, solid-foam cushions stay damp for two days or more and smell of chlorine. For choice by surface: PTFE or light polyamide glide on slab, stone and tiling — slides without marking but grips poorly on wet ground; studded EPDM glide on composite and timber — good grip but may mark light floors; filled polypropylene glide on concrete and compacted gravel — resistant and economical but crushes under heavy load; ballasted base on gravel and coping — stable and removable but bulky and heavy in logistics.
Which specifications and tests to require in an outdoor furniture tender?

An outdoor tender is judged on five documents: the reports of EN 581-1, EN 581-2 and EN 581-3 tests, the salt-spray and coating-adhesion test records, the assembly sheet with the anchoring plan, the spare-parts list and the approved sample. Without these five documents, the compared price compares nothing, and the best offer on paper becomes the costliest in use. The EN 581 series covers outdoor furniture for domestic, communal and camping use: part 1 covers general safety requirements, part 2 seats, part 3 tables. The corresponding test methods, notably EN 1728 for seating and EN 1022 for stability, say how loads are applied, how tipping is tested and how measurements are taken. A serious supplier cites them with the laboratory and the report date; a supplier who answers 'compliant with European standards' without a report number has no report. Powder coating is documented by two tests: salt spray per ISO 9227, with a duration depending on the target class, and adhesion per ISO 2409, with an expected class of 1 or better. For woven pieces, request the UV ageing report per ISO 4892-3 and the HDPE composition. For timber, request the species, origin, moisture content before machining and, where applicable, the chain-of-custody certificate. Three clauses deserve to be written black on white in the contract: spare-parts availability duration, expressed in years and not 'subject to stock'; the warranty structure, split between frame, finish and weaving, because a single five-year warranty often hides a finish exclusion; the sample approval procedure, with a validation lead time and a clear rule on colour variation between prototype and series. Manufacturing control is also verified: a supplier audit per ISO 9001 documents a system, not a batch; ask in addition for the batch control plan, coating-thickness records and treatment-bath traceability. The thresholds to request, item by item: general safety EN 581-1, dated report with identified laboratory; outdoor seating EN 581-2, compliant load and stability; outdoor tables EN 581-3, stability test included; salt spray ISO 9227, duration per class and report of the delivered batch; coating adhesion ISO 2409, class 1 or better; UV ageing ISO 4892-3, report on the delivered HDPE.
How to build a coherent package across terrace, pool deck and garden?

A coherent terrace and pool furniture package is built by zone: the covered terrace favours comfort and the warmth of timber, the pool deck favours aluminium and resin for lightness and fast drying, the garden favours robustness and ground anchoring. Coherence does not come from a single material applied everywhere; it comes from a palette, a vocabulary of shapes and a finish level held from one zone to the next. Piece counts follow operations, not the architect's plan: the ratio sits rather between 0.6 and 1.2 loungers per room depending on the number of pools and the clientele, and a restaurant terrace needs a cover count equal to seated capacity plus a 10–15% reserve for breakage and replacement. These ratios are checked with the operator before the quantities are frozen, because they also determine the size of the storage area. Storage is the poor relation of outdoor packages: a stack of ten loungers occupies about 1.5–2.5 m² of floor, provided the geometry allows it; a badly designed folding table takes more room than a fixed one. In an urban hotel, storage is often an unventilated technical room where cushions stay damp; breathable covers and low-level ventilation cost less than replacing the foam after two years. The finish palette is locked early: two different suppliers on the same pool deck produce two shades of grey because of the powder batch, and the difference shows in full sun. If the package is phased, either order all the powder at once or accept a written colour tolerance. The hotel furniture checklist helps not to forget the accessory pieces — ashtrays, beach trolleys, poolside racks — which carry little value and many complaints. Finally, the outdoor package must plan its own renewal: a pool-deck chair is often replaced by two or three units each season, not thirty. Keeping the reference, shade and technical sheet of the batch allows unit orders three years later. By zone: covered terrace — armchairs and low tables, comfort and warm touch, teak or black locust; pool deck — loungers, tables and parasols, drying, weight and washing, aluminium and resin; garden — benches and dining tables, anchoring and robustness, black locust or aluminium; private beach — low loungers and trolleys, sand, wind and storage, aluminium or light resin. Hongye Furniture Group has supported hotel projects since 1996 with outdoor ranges produced under the same control requirements as indoor furniture; for a terrace and pool package, the FF&E team works from plans, quantities and anchoring constraints, then provides assembly sheets, test reports and samples before launch, with sample confirmation following the documented procedure that locks shade, material and finish before the series.

Fixing type per substrate: slab, joist, gravel, lawn, pool coping
